entries.caption: GnRH from the hypothalamus reaches the anterior pituitary through connecting blood vessels. FSH travels in blood to Sertoli cells and supports their contribution to germ-cell development. LH travels in blood to interstitial cells, which release testosterone. Local testosterone also supports sperm development. These arrows indicate signalling and support; FSH and LH do not become testosterone.
entries.scientificReview: Native1200x900 reviewed: hypothalamic GnRH enters anterior pituitary; split FSH/Sertoli and LH/interstitial branches are distinct; testosterone joins local developmental support. All labels and arrows fit with no crossing interpreted as a junction.
limitations: Diagram is a causal simplification, not anatomy at scale or measurement evidence.

entries.caption: The upper loop combines hypothalamic input with anterior-pituitary LH release. LH stimulates interstitial cells; testosterone can reduce upstream hypothalamic and pituitary signalling. The lower loop isolates FSH support of Sertoli cells and inhibin feedback that reduces pituitary FSH release. Arrowheads show support; blunt ends show inhibition. Lower testosterone action can permit increased LH when upstream tissues respond, but one measurement does not establish a unique cause.

entries.caption: Cervical stretch during labour sends sensory signals associated with oxytocin release. Hypothalamic neurons make oxytocin; it is stored and released through the posterior pituitary into blood. Responsive uterine tissue contracts, which can increase cervical stretch and reinforce this loop. Delivery removes the main stretch stimulus. This is one mechanism within labour; it does not claim that fetal size alone starts labour or that the loop explains all timing and tissue responses.

entries.caption: Suckling provides sensory input supporting both pathways. Anterior-pituitary prolactin supports milk synthesis by milk-producing cells. Oxytocin, made in hypothalamic neurons and released through posterior pituitary, supports contraction of myoepithelial cells around secretory tissue, helping eject existing milk. After placental delivery, falling steroid levels support greater synthesis; prolactin is not first created only after birth. Synthesis, ejection and effective transfer are related but distinct outcomes.
